opus-5.5.text:
I think it's genuinely valuable, and in some ways it gets at something our more controlled measurements can't. When we build benchmarks or run something like a randomized controlled trial, we're choosing the tasks, the setting, the time limits, and all of those choices introduce some artificiality. Looking at how people actually use these tools in the wild tells you what they're choosing to use AI for, how often, and in what contexts, and that's real signal about where the value is.

But I'd be pretty cautious about treating usage as a direct measure of helpfulness. The core issue is that usage and benefit can come apart quite a bit. People's perceptions of how much AI is speeding them up aren't always reliable. In our work looking at experienced open-source developers, one of the striking things was the gap between how much faster developers expected to be, and believed they had been, and what we actually measured. If you'd only looked at their usage patterns, or asked them, you'd have concluded AI was helping a lot, and the measured effect pointed in a different direction, at least in that setting.

There are a few reasons for that. Using AI can feel productive, since it's less effortful, more engaging, and you're always getting output, even when the end-to-end time or quality isn't better. There's selection too: people reach for AI on tasks where they think it'll help, which isn't the same as where it actually helps. And usage logs mostly capture the interaction, not the counterfactual. You see someone accept a suggestion, but not whether they'd have written something better faster without it, or how much time they spent reviewing and fixing things afterward.

So I see usage data as complementary. It's great for generating hypotheses, understanding the distribution of real tasks, and checking whether lab results are ecologically valid. But to make causal claims about how much AI is helping, you really want some counterfactual comparison, whether that's randomization, careful natural experiments, or at least objective outcome measures rather than self-reports. Ideally you triangulate: benchmarks, RCTs, and real-world usage each have different failure modes, and when they agree you can be more confident, and when they disagree, that disagreement is itself really informative.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says usage and benefit can come apart, and that people may use AI or feel it helps even when measured outcomes show otherwise.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there's a lot of value in it, but I also think it has some pretty important limitations that are worth being clear about.

The appeal is obvious. If you look at what people are actually doing with these systems, you get away from the artificiality of benchmarks. Benchmarks are these constructed tasks where we've decided ahead of time what the right answer is, and it's always been a question how much that transfers to the messy stuff people actually want help with. Real usage data is grounded in things people care enough about to actually try. So as a signal of where the models are being used, and what kinds of tasks they seem useful for, that's really informative.

The problem is that usage is not the same thing as benefit. People use things for all sorts of reasons. Something can be engaging, or feel helpful, without actually making you more productive or improving the quality of your output. And there's a selection effect baked in. You only see the tasks people chose to bring to the model, which are presumably the ones they already expected it to do well on. You don't see the tasks they didn't bother with because they assumed it would fail. So you get a picture that's biased toward the model's strengths.

The other thing I'd flag is that the person using the system is often not in a great position to judge how much it helped them. If you ask a developer how much faster they were with an AI tool, their estimate can be pretty far off from what you'd measure if you actually ran a controlled comparison. People anchor on the experience of the interaction, which can feel fast and smooth, rather than the end-to-end time including all the fixing and verifying afterward. So if your usage data is relying on self-reports of helpfulness, you inherit that problem.

So I'd say the right way to think about it is as one input among several. Usage patterns tell you where to look. They tell you what people want and what they're trying. But to actually measure how much the AI is helping, you need something closer to an experiment, where you can compare against what would have happened without it. The two approaches are kind of complementary. Usage data gives you ecological validity and tells you what matters in practice, and controlled studies give you the causal story. Neither one on its own really answers the question.

r001.rationale: The candidate explicitly says that usage is not the same as benefit and explains that people may use AI without becoming more productive or improving their output.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a useful source of evidence, but there’s a pretty big gap between observing that someone uses an AI system and knowing how much it helps them. If someone keeps coming back to it, that suggests they’re getting some value out of it. But it doesn’t tell you whether they’re producing better work, saving time, or spending more time checking and correcting what the model gives them.

The key question is the counterfactual: what would they have done without the AI? They might have done the task themselves, asked someone else, or simply not done it. Those possibilities give you very different interpretations of the same usage pattern.

So I’d want to combine usage data with something that measures outcomes, ideally a comparison where some people have access and others don’t. Usage patterns can tell us which tasks matter to people and where to look for benefits. I’m less confident that they can, by themselves, tell us the size of those benefits.

r001.rationale: The response says that observing use—even repeated use—does not establish that AI is helping or improving outcomes.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s useful evidence, but there’s a pretty big gap between observing that someone uses an AI system and knowing how much it helps them. If somebody keeps coming back to a tool, especially if they’re paying for it, that tells you they perceive some benefit. It doesn’t directly tell you how much better their work is, or how much time they’re saving.

The difficulty is the counterfactual: what would they have done without the system? They might have done the same task more slowly, asked another person, or just not done it at all. Those cases imply pretty different kinds of value, and usage data alone doesn’t distinguish them.

So I’d want to combine usage patterns with experiments where you can compare outcomes with and without AI. Usage tells you which tasks people actually care about and where to look. Then you need some separate way of checking whether the assistance actually improves the outcome.

r001.rationale: The response says that repeated use suggests users perceive a benefit but does not establish that AI improves their work or saves time, distinguishing usage from actual help.
